opus-5.5.text:
I think the prospects are actually quite good, but with an important caveat: I don't believe the traditional methods will work if we simply copy them over unchanged.

When I say "physics of AI," I mean treating neural networks the way physicists treat natural systems. You observe phenomena, form simple hypotheses, design controlled experiments, and try to find the minimal model that captures the essence. That spirit is very much traditional physics, and I think it's underused in AI right now. A lot of the field is driven by engineering: scale up, try a new architecture, see if the benchmark goes up. That's been enormously productive, but it leaves a big gap in understanding. We often don't know *why* things work.

Take grokking, which I've worked on. Models suddenly generalize long after they've memorized the training data. You can study that with toy models, like modular arithmetic, where everything is small enough to visualize. You can look at the learned representations and see structure emerge, almost like a phase transition. That's a very physics-style approach: strip the problem down until you can actually see what's going on.

But there are real challenges. In physics, nature is fixed. The laws don't change because someone published a new paper. In AI, the "nature" we're studying is something we build, and it changes every few months. So there's a risk that by the time you understand one phenomenon carefully, the field has moved on. That means physics of AI has to focus on things that are universal, phenomena that persist across architectures and scales, like scaling laws, representation geometry, or certain training dynamics. If you find something that holds no matter how the model is built, that's where physics-style understanding pays off.

Another difference is that the traditional pipeline in physics, where theory and experiment are often done by different people over long timescales, may be too slow here. In AI, the experimentalist and the theorist can be the same person, and an experiment can take an afternoon on a GPU. So I think the methodology should be more like "fast physics": quick cycles of observation, hypothesis, and testing, with toy models as the main tool.

There's also a cultural point. Physicists are trained to be comfortable with approximations and with saying "this is not rigorous, but it captures the main effect." Mathematicians want proofs, and engineers want performance. Physics sits in between, and I think AI really needs that middle ground right now. We need effective theories, not necessarily first-principles derivations of everything.

So overall I'm optimistic. I think in ten or twenty years, people will look back and see that understanding these systems required something like a new branch of physics, and the people who started building it with simple models and careful observation were doing valuable work, even when it looked small compared to training giant models.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about progress over the next ten or twenty years and says traditional research cycles may be too slow; it does not suggest development could take centuries.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Aristotle’s era or express uncertainty about whether physics of AI has reached a comparable developmental stage.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm fairly optimistic, actually, but I think we have to be honest about what "traditional research methods" means here. When I say "physics of AI," I'm not trying to claim that a neural network is literally a physical system. I'm borrowing the way physicists approach a problem: you find a simple, controlled setting, you look for order parameters, you build a toy model that captures the essential mechanism, and then you check whether the predictions survive when you scale up.

That style of working has already paid off. Scaling laws are basically an empirical physics result. Phase transitions in training, like grokking, look a lot like the phenomena people study in statistical mechanics. Neural scaling, feature learning, the lottery ticket phenomenon, mechanistic interpretability, all of these have been approached productively with the physicist's toolbox of simplification plus careful experiments.

The reason I'm hopeful is that neural networks are, in a sense, better than real physical systems for doing science. We can measure every weight, every activation, at every training step. We can rerun the universe with a different random seed. In physics you spend billions of dollars building a collider to observe one process. Here, you can run a thousand controlled experiments on a laptop. So the observational side is actually much easier than physics ever had.

The hard part is the theory side. Physics got lucky in that nature has a small number of fundamental laws, and symmetry constrains almost everything. Neural networks are engineered objects, and the "laws" may depend on architecture, data, optimizer, and all sorts of choices. So I don't expect a single grand unified theory of deep learning in the way we have the Standard Model. What I expect instead is something closer to condensed matter physics: a collection of effective theories, each valid in some regime, that explain a cluster of phenomena and make useful predictions.

There's also a cultural tension. Traditional physics research moves slowly and carefully, with a lot of emphasis on understanding before building. AI moves at a pace where the empirical frontier shifts every six months. If you take three years to perfectly understand a two-layer network, the field may have moved on. So the physics of AI has to adopt a faster, more experimental loop than physics usually does, while keeping the discipline of asking "what's the mechanism" rather than just "what's the benchmark number."

So my answer is: the methods transfer well, the attitude transfers well, but the ambition needs to be recalibrated. We should aim for a good set of effective theories and a culture of controlled experiments, and I think over the next decade that will genuinely change how people design and train models, not just how they explain them after the fact.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic that the work will change model design over the next decade; it does not suggest development could take centuries.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses effective theories and the pace of AI research but makes no comparison to Aristotle’s era or uncertainty about reaching that stage.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we have to be careful about what we mean by a physics of AI. To me, it means finding a small set of principles that explain how complicated behavior emerges from relatively simple learning rules. Traditional physics gives us a useful way to approach that: observe a phenomenon, build a simplified model, and test whether the model makes predictions beyond the observations that inspired it.

The challenge is choosing what to simplify. If you make a neural network analytically tractable but remove the thing responsible for its interesting behavior, you may solve a beautiful problem without learning much about AI. So I think theory and experiments have to stay very close. We need simple systems that still exhibit the phenomenon we want to understand, and then we need to check whether the explanation carries over to larger systems.

I wouldn’t expect one theory to explain everything immediately. Progress may begin with understanding individual phenomena—why a particular capability appears, or why a change in training produces a different kind of solution. If those explanations eventually connect, that’s how a broader physics of AI could emerge.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic about progress but does not suggest it could take centuries.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare AI physics to Aristotle’s era or express uncertainty about reaching that stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think traditional research methods can take us quite far, but we need to be careful about what we’re trying to explain. In physics, we often start with a complicated phenomenon, find a simplified system that preserves something essential, and then move back and forth between experiments and theory. I think that approach is useful for AI, too.

For example, instead of trying to explain an entire language model at once, we can study a particular learning behavior in a small model. We can vary the conditions, identify a pattern, and ask whether there’s a simple mechanism behind it. Then we have to check whether that mechanism still matters in larger, more realistic systems.

The danger is that we make a beautiful theory of a toy model and assume we’ve explained AI. The connection to actual systems has to be tested. So I’m optimistic about the methods, but I wouldn’t assume the answers will look exactly like the physics we already know. We should let the phenomena guide us.
